courseDetails.title: General Physics II
courseDetails.description: A 100-level course covering electric charge, electric fields and potential, capacitance, direct and alternating-current circuits, magnetism, electromagnetic induction, waves, inductance, and transformers.

questions.question: Which statement best defines electric charge?
options: A measure of the temperature of a conductor
The rate at which an object performs mechanical work
The amount of mass contained in an object
A property of matter that causes it to experience electric forces
questions.explanation: Electric charge is a fundamental property of matter responsible for electric attraction and repulsion.

questions.question: How do two positively charged particles interact when brought close together?
options: They exchange protons until their charges reverse
questions.explanation: Like charges repel, whereas unlike charges attract.

questions.question: Why is an ordinary uncharged object described as electrically neutral?
options: Its protons have no electric charge
It contains no protons or electrons
It contains equal total positive and negative charge
questions.explanation: A neutral object normally has equal positive charge from protons and negative charge from electrons.

questions.question: What happens to the net charge of a neutral object when it gains electrons?
options: It remains neutral in every case
questions.explanation: Electrons carry negative charge, so gaining electrons produces an excess of negative charge.

questions.question: What does the quantisation of electric charge mean?
options: Charge can have any value with no smallest unit
Only positive charge can be measured
Electric charge is always uniformly distributed
Charge occurs in integer multiples of the elementary charge
questions.explanation: Quantisation means q = ne, where n is an integer and e is the elementary charge, approximately 1.6 × 10^-19 C in magnitude.

questions.question: Which statement expresses conservation of electric charge?
options: The total charge of an isolated system remains constant
The charge of an electron increases with speed
Charge disappears whenever two opposite charges meet
Positive charge can be created without an equal change elsewhere
questions.explanation: Charge may be transferred between bodies, but the total charge in an isolated system does not change.

questions.question: When two different materials are rubbed together and electrons move from one to the other, the charging method is called what?
questions.explanation: Frictional charging results from electron transfer when two materials are rubbed together.

questions.question: Which feature distinguishes charging by induction from charging by conduction?
options: Induction can charge an object without direct contact with the charged body
Induction requires both bodies to be rubbed together
Conduction always leaves the neutral body oppositely charged
questions.explanation: Conduction involves direct contact, while induction uses charge separation and usually grounding without contact with the inducing charge.

questions.question: According to Coulomb's law, the magnitude of the force between two point charges is proportional to what?
options: The product of the charges divided by the square of their separation
The difference between the charges divided by their separation
The sum of the charges multiplied by their separation
The product of the charges multiplied by the square of their separation
questions.explanation: Coulomb's law is F = k|q1q2|/r^2.

questions.question: Two charges of +2 μC and +3 μC are separated by 0.30 m. Using k = 9.0 × 10^9 N·m^2/C^2, what is the force between them?
questions.explanation: F = kq1q2/r^2 = (9.0 × 10^9)(2 × 10^-6)(3 × 10^-6)/(0.30)^2 = 0.60 N. Both charges are positive, so the force is repulsive.

questions.question: The force between two point charges is 200 N. If their separation is doubled while the charges remain unchanged, what is the new force?
questions.explanation: Because F is proportional to 1/r^2, doubling r reduces the force by 2^2 = 4: 200/4 = 50 N.

questions.question: What does the principle of superposition state for several electric forces acting on one charge?
options: The net force is the vector sum of the individual forces
Only the force from the nearest charge is considered
All forces cancel regardless of direction
questions.explanation: Each source charge acts independently, and the resultant is found by vector addition.

questions.question: A 2.0 C test charge experiences an electric force of 10,500 N. What is the electric-field magnitude?
What is the electric-field magnitude 0.30 m from a +4.0 nC point charge? Use k = 9.0 × 10^9 N·m^2/C^2.
What is the direction of the electric field produced by an isolated negative point charge?
questions.explanation: Electric-field direction is defined by the force on a positive test charge, which is attracted toward a negative source charge.

questions.question: What does a greater density of electric-field lines in a diagram indicate?
options: A reversal of the source charge
A region of zero potential only
questions.explanation: Closely spaced field lines represent greater field magnitude.

questions.question: A uniform electric field of 200 N/C points east. What force acts on an electron of charge -1.6 × 10^-19 C?
options: 0 N because an electron is a point particle
questions.explanation: F = qE. The magnitude is (1.6 × 10^-19)(200) = 3.2 × 10^-17 N. A negative charge experiences force opposite the field, so the force is west.

questions.question: Why are metals generally good electrical conductors?
options: Their protons move freely between atoms
They contain charge carriers that can move relatively freely
questions.explanation: In conductors, mobile electrons can move through the material under an electric field.

questions.question: Which statement best describes an electrical insulator?
options: It strongly resists the movement of electric charge
It allows electrons to flow as freely as a metal
questions.explanation: Insulators have very few mobile charge carriers and therefore high resistance to charge flow.

questions.question: What is the electric field inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium?
options: Equal to the field just outside in every direction
Dependent only on the conductor's mass
questions.explanation: Free charges redistribute until the internal electric field becomes zero.

questions.question: Capacitance is defined by which relationship?
questions.explanation: Capacitance is charge stored per unit potential difference: C = Q/V.

questions.question: A 5 μF capacitor is connected across a 12 V battery. How much charge is stored?
Two capacitors of 3 μF and 5 μF are connected in parallel. What is their equivalent capacitance?
questions.explanation: Parallel capacitances add directly: Ceq = 3 + 5 = 8 μF.

questions.question: Two capacitors of 10 μF and 20 μF are connected in series. What is their equivalent capacitance?
questions.explanation: For two series capacitors, Ceq = C1C2/(C1 + C2) = (10 × 20)/30 = 6.67 μF.

questions.question: What is the energy stored in a 2 μF capacitor charged to 100 V?
What is the main effect of inserting a dielectric of relative permittivity κ fully between the plates of an isolated parallel-plate capacitor?
options: Its capacitance increases by a factor of κ
Its plate area decreases by a factor of κ
Its stored charge must reverse sign
questions.explanation: A dielectric polarises and reduces the effective field for a given charge, increasing capacitance to C = κC0.

questions.question: Electromotive force, ε, is best defined as what?
options: Energy supplied by a source per unit charge
questions.explanation: EMF is the work or energy supplied by the source per coulomb, measured in volts.

questions.question: For a cell of EMF ε and internal resistance r delivering current I, what is its terminal voltage?
questions.explanation: While the cell supplies current, Ir is the voltage lost inside the source, so V = ε - Ir.

questions.question: A battery has EMF 12 V and internal resistance 1 Ω. If it supplies 2 A, what is its terminal voltage?
A charge of 2 C has electric potential energy of 20 J at a point. What is the electric potential there?
A 0.70 m conducting rod moves at 1.0 m/s perpendicular to a 20 T magnetic field. What motional EMF is produced?
questions.explanation: For perpendicular motion, |ε| = BLv = (20)(0.70)(1.0) = 14 V.

questions.question: An electric dipole consists of charges ±5 nC separated by 2 cm. What is its dipole moment magnitude?
An electric dipole with p = 3 × 10^-3 C·m is placed at 90° in an electric field of 2,000 N/C. What torque acts on it?
questions.explanation: τ = pE sinθ = (3 × 10^-3)(2000)sin90° = 6 N·m. The torque is maximum at 90°.

questions.question: Which equation states Ohm's law for an ohmic resistor?
questions.explanation: Ohm's law relates potential difference, current, and resistance as V = IR.

questions.question: Resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω, and 6 Ω are connected in series. What is the total resistance?
questions.explanation: Series resistances add: Rtotal = 2 + 3 + 6 = 11 Ω.

questions.question: Resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω, and 6 Ω are connected in parallel. What is their equivalent resistance?
A 10 V battery is connected to 2 Ω and 3 Ω resistors in series. What current flows?
questions.explanation: Rtotal = 2 + 3 = 5 Ω, so I = V/R = 10/5 = 2 A.

questions.question: A 5 Ω resistor carries a current of 2 A. What power does it dissipate?
What is the equivalent resistance of 4 Ω and 12 Ω connected in parallel?
Three resistors of 5 Ω, 10 Ω, and 15 Ω are in series across 60 V. What is the circuit current?
questions.explanation: Rtotal = 30 Ω, so I = 60/30 = 2 A.

questions.question: Kirchhoff's current law is based on which principle?
questions.explanation: At a junction, the total current entering equals the total current leaving because charge does not accumulate there.

questions.question: Currents of 5 A and 3 A enter a junction. If there is only one outgoing branch, what current leaves the junction?
questions.explanation: By Kirchhoff's current law, Iout = 5 + 3 = 8 A.

questions.question: According to Kirchhoff's voltage law, what is the algebraic sum of potential changes around a closed loop?
questions.explanation: Kirchhoff's voltage law expresses conservation of energy: the algebraic sum of all rises and drops in a loop is zero.

questions.question: A circuit loop contains a 20 V battery and known voltage drops of 5 V and 10 V. What additional voltage drop completes the loop?
questions.explanation: KVL gives 20 - 5 - 10 - V = 0, so V = 5 V.

questions.question: A battery has EMF 12 V and terminal voltage 10 V while supplying 2 A. What is its internal resistance?
For the alternating voltage v = 20 sin(50t) V, what is the peak voltage?
questions.explanation: In v = V0 sin(ωt), the coefficient V0 is the peak value, so V0 = 20 V.

questions.question: The instantaneous current is i = 30 sin(50t) A. What is its RMS value?
A household supply has an RMS voltage of 120 V. What is its approximate peak voltage?
An AC device operates at 220 V RMS and 5.0 A RMS. What are the corresponding peak values?
questions.explanation: Peak values are √2 times RMS values: V0 ≈ 311 V and I0 ≈ 7.07 A.

questions.question: What is the phase relationship between voltage and current in a purely resistive AC circuit?
questions.explanation: For a pure resistor, voltage and current reach zero and maximum values together.

questions.question: In a purely inductive AC circuit, how does current relate to voltage?
options: Current is in phase with voltage
questions.explanation: For an ideal inductor, voltage leads current by 90°, so current lags voltage.

questions.question: In a purely capacitive AC circuit, how does current relate to voltage?
options: Current is in phase with voltage
questions.explanation: For an ideal capacitor, current reaches its maximum one-quarter cycle before voltage.

questions.question: What is the inductive reactance of a 0.10 H inductor connected to a 50 Hz supply?
In a series RLC circuit, I = 3 mA, R = 1000 Ω, VL = 30 V, and VC = 18 V. What is the supply voltage?
questions.explanation: VR = IR = 0.003(1000) = 3 V. The net reactive voltage is 30 - 18 = 12 V, so V = √(3^2 + 12^2) = √153 ≈ 12.37 V.

questions.question: What does a phasor represent in AC circuit analysis?
options: The magnitude and phase of a sinusoidal quantity
Only the instantaneous resistance of a circuit
A constant DC voltage with no direction
The total charge that passes in one cycle
questions.explanation: A phasor is a rotating-vector representation used to compare sinusoidal magnitudes and phase angles.

questions.question: What is the resonance condition in a series RLC circuit?
questions.explanation: At resonance, inductive and capacitive reactances cancel, leaving a purely resistive impedance.

questions.question: A series RLC circuit has L = 0.10 H and C = 100 μF. What is its resonant frequency?
At resonance, what is the impedance of an ideal series RLC circuit?
options: It is zero regardless of R
questions.explanation: Since XL - XC = 0 at resonance, Z = √(R^2 + 0^2) = R.

questions.question: What is the power factor of a series RLC circuit at resonance?
options: It depends only on the value of the capacitor
questions.explanation: At resonance, voltage and current are in phase, so cosφ = 1. Doubling R does not change this resonance power factor.

questions.question: Which expression gives average power in a sinusoidal AC circuit?
questions.explanation: Average AC power is the product of RMS voltage, RMS current, and the power factor cosφ.

questions.question: What is the average power consumed by an ideal inductor or ideal capacitor over a complete AC cycle?
questions.explanation: Ideal reactive components store and return energy; with a 90° phase difference, cos90° = 0.

questions.question: A series RLC circuit has R = 6 Ω and impedance Z = 10 Ω. What is its power factor?
questions.explanation: Power factor cosφ = R/Z = 6/10 = 0.60.

questions.question: Outside a bar magnet, in what direction do magnetic-field lines run?
options: Clockwise around both poles regardless of orientation
In straight lines that end midway between the poles
From the north pole to the south pole
From the south pole to the north pole only
questions.explanation: Magnetic-field lines emerge from the north pole and enter the south pole outside the magnet, forming closed loops.

questions.question: What happens when a bar magnet is cut into two pieces?
options: One piece becomes only north and the other only south
Each piece becomes electrically charged but nonmagnetic
Each piece becomes a smaller magnet with north and south poles
Both pieces lose all magnetism immediately
questions.explanation: Magnetic poles occur in pairs; cutting a magnet produces smaller dipoles rather than isolated poles.

questions.question: What is the magnetic dipole moment of a single-turn current loop of area A carrying current I?
questions.explanation: For one turn, magnetic dipole moment equals current times loop area; for N turns, μ = NIA.

questions.question: At what angle between magnetic dipole moment μ and magnetic field B is the torque maximum?
questions.explanation: τ = μB sinθ, which is maximum when sinθ = 1 at 90°.

questions.question: What is the magnitude of the magnetic force on a charge q moving with speed v at angle θ to a magnetic field B?
questions.explanation: The magnetic part of the Lorentz force depends on the component of velocity perpendicular to B.

questions.question: When does a moving charged particle experience zero magnetic force in a nonzero uniform magnetic field?
options: Only when its charge is positive
Whenever its velocity is perpendicular to the field
When its velocity is parallel or antiparallel to the field
questions.explanation: F = |q|vB sinθ; for θ = 0° or 180°, sinθ = 0.

questions.question: Which equation gives the total Lorentz force on a charge in electric and magnetic fields?
questions.explanation: The Lorentz force combines the electric force qE and magnetic force q(v × B).

questions.question: Why does a magnetic force alone do no work on a charged particle?
options: The force is always parallel to displacement
Every charged particle has zero mass
The force is perpendicular to the particle's velocity
The magnetic field has no direction
questions.explanation: A perpendicular force changes the direction of velocity but not the particle's speed or kinetic energy.

questions.question: A 2 C charge moves at 3 m/s perpendicular to a 4 T magnetic field. What magnetic force acts on it?
How are the electric field, magnetic field, and direction of travel related in an electromagnetic wave?
options: Only the magnetic field has a direction
All three directions are mutually perpendicular
The electric and magnetic fields are parallel but perpendicular to travel
questions.explanation: An electromagnetic wave is transverse: E is perpendicular to B, and both are perpendicular to propagation.

questions.question: Which equation relates electromagnetic-wave speed c, frequency f, and wavelength λ in vacuum?
questions.explanation: Wave speed equals frequency multiplied by wavelength.

questions.question: Which sequence lists electromagnetic radiation in order of increasing frequency?
options: Radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma ray
Gamma ray, X-ray, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwave, radio
Microwave, radio, visible, infrared, ultraviolet, gamma ray, X-ray
Radio, infrared, microwave, visible, X-ray, ultraviolet, gamma ray
questions.explanation: Frequency increases from radio waves through microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays.

questions.question: What is the wavelength in vacuum of a 100 MHz electromagnetic wave? Use c = 3.0 × 10^8 m/s.
Why can electromagnetic waves travel through empty space?
options: They are mechanical vibrations of a material medium
Their speed becomes zero in a vacuum
They require air molecules to carry electric charge
They consist of self-propagating changing electric and magnetic fields
questions.explanation: Unlike mechanical waves, electromagnetic waves do not require a material medium.

questions.question: In an ideal LC oscillator, energy continually changes between which two forms?
options: Electric energy in the capacitor and magnetic energy in the inductor
Thermal energy and chemical energy only
Kinetic energy of the resistor and elastic energy of the wire
questions.explanation: The capacitor stores electric-field energy and the inductor stores magnetic-field energy.

questions.question: If the frequency of an electromagnetic wave in vacuum is doubled, what happens to its wavelength?
questions.explanation: Since c = fλ is constant in vacuum, λ is inversely proportional to f.

questions.question: What is self-inductance?
options: The cancellation of all magnetic fields in a coil
The production of an EMF in a circuit by a change in its own current
The flow of steady current through a pure resistor
The production of charge by rubbing two insulators
questions.explanation: A changing current changes the coil's magnetic flux and induces an opposing EMF in the same circuit.

questions.question: Which expression gives the self-induced EMF of an inductor?
questions.explanation: The self-induced EMF is proportional to the rate of change of current, with the minus sign expressing Lenz's law.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of inductance?
questions.explanation: Inductance is measured in henries, symbol H.

questions.question: How much energy is stored in a 0.20 H inductor carrying 3.0 A?
What is mutual inductance?
options: A capacitor stores charge on two plates
A changing current in one circuit induces an EMF in another circuit
A magnet loses both poles when divided
Two resistors share the same current in series
questions.explanation: Mutual inductance describes magnetic coupling between two circuits or coils.

questions.question: Two coils have mutual inductance 0.50 H. If the current in the first changes at 4.0 A/s, what is the induced-EMF magnitude in the second?
Which change generally increases the inductance of a coil?
options: Replacing the coil with a straight resistor
Reducing the number of turns to zero
Increasing the number of turns and inserting a ferromagnetic core
Removing all magnetic flux from the coil
questions.explanation: More turns and a high-permeability core increase flux linkage for a given current, thereby increasing inductance.

questions.question: A uniform electric field of 2 N/C crosses a flat area of 1 m^2 at 30° to the area vector. What is the electric flux?
What does Gauss's law state for a closed surface?
options: The net electric flux equals the enclosed charge divided by ε0
The enclosed charge equals ε0 divided by flux
The net electric flux always equals zero
The electric field equals the surface area divided by charge
questions.explanation: Gauss's law is ∮E·dA = Qenclosed/ε0.

questions.question: A closed surface is placed in an external electric field but encloses no net charge. What is its net electric flux?
questions.explanation: Field lines may enter and leave, but Gauss's law gives net flux Qenclosed/ε0 = 0.

questions.question: Which expression represents Faraday's law for a coil of N turns?
questions.explanation: The induced EMF equals the negative rate of change of magnetic-flux linkage.

questions.question: What does the negative sign in Faraday's law represent?
options: The induced effect opposes the change in magnetic flux
The induced voltage is always numerically negative
The coil must contain negative charge
questions.explanation: The minus sign is Lenz's law: the induced current creates a magnetic effect that opposes the change producing it.

questions.question: A bar magnet is held stationary inside a stationary coil. What induced EMF is produced?
options: An EMF that increases without limit
An alternating EMF even with no motion
Zero, because the magnetic flux is not changing
questions.explanation: Faraday's law requires changing magnetic flux; a static magnet and coil produce no induced EMF.

questions.question: Which action increases the magnitude of the EMF induced in a coil?
options: Making the magnetic field weaker and moving more slowly
Holding the magnet and coil completely stationary
Reducing the number of turns while keeping all else fixed
Increasing the number of turns or changing the magnetic flux more rapidly
questions.explanation: |ε| = N|dΦB/dt|, so more turns or a faster flux change increases the EMF.

questions.question: The electric potential is V(x) = 3x^2 - x^3. What is the x-component of the electric field at x = 2?
What are the three main parts of a basic transformer?
options: Primary coil, secondary coil, and iron core
Input coil, output coil, and capacitor
Voltage coil, current coil, and permanent magnet
Primary coil, secondary coil, and battery
questions.explanation: A basic transformer has primary and secondary windings magnetically linked by a core.

questions.question: On what principle does a transformer operate?
options: Mutual induction produced by alternating magnetic flux
questions.explanation: Alternating current in the primary creates changing core flux, which induces EMF in the secondary.

questions.question: For an ideal transformer, which turns-ratio relation is correct?
questions.explanation: The secondary-to-primary voltage ratio equals the secondary-to-primary turns ratio.

questions.question: Which condition describes a step-up transformer?
questions.explanation: More turns on the secondary produce a higher secondary voltage.

questions.question: Which relationship holds for an ideal transformer with no power loss?
questions.explanation: Input power equals output power in an ideal transformer. Consequently, voltage and current change inversely.

questions.question: A transformer has 600 primary turns and changes 240 V to 120 V. How many secondary turns are required?
Why is the iron core of a transformer commonly laminated?
options: To increase electrical conduction between core layers
To make the transformer operate on direct current
To eliminate the need for a secondary winding
questions.explanation: Insulated laminations interrupt circulating eddy-current paths and improve transformer efficiency.
